children.prompt: The volume of three identical cube shaped containers is $18\text{ m}^3$. Calculate the side length of one of the cubes in exact form.

answer.worked:
Let the side length of each cube be $x$ metres.
$$\begin{align*}3x^3&=18\\x^3&=6\\x&=\sqrt[3]{6}\end{align*}$$
The side length is $\sqrt[3]{6}\text{ m}$.

content.prompt: A rectangular prism has dimensions in ratio $1:2:3$. Calculate the side lengths if the volume is $4374\text{ cm}^3$.

answer.worked:
Let the side lengths be $x$, $2x$ and $3x$ centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}x\times2x\times3x&=4374\\6x^3&=4374\\x^3&=729\\x&=\sqrt[3]{729}\\x&=9\end{align*}$$
The side lengths are $9\text{ cm}$, $18\text{ cm}$ and $27\text{ cm}$.

[Pedagogy review · High priority · example-choice · pf-0714dca4da]
Finding: All worked and guided examples have integer roots, so the teaching never demonstrates retaining a non-integer cube root as an exact answer and giving its decimal approximation.
Breakdown: The examples permit the wrong rule that cube rooting always finishes with an integer. Students encounter no modelled exact stopping point before p4-q1-k, while p4-q2-b explicitly requires exact form.
Checked: The complete teaching states the general cube-root method but contains no worked example, guided question or explicit contrast exposing this distinction. Practice questions and their answers do not supply that teaching. ∛28≈3.03659, so 3.04 is correct to two decimal places.
Assumes: A calculator is available, inferred from the requests for decimal approximations. Calculator operation is not treated as a missing prerequisite.
Also affects: p3-example-2, p3-guided-practice, p4-q1-k, p4-q2-b
Proposed repair (change-values): Change p3-example-1 to x³=28 and show: 'x=∛28 (exact); x≈3.04 (to 2 d.p., using a calculator). This cube root is not an integer, so retain ∛28 for the exact answer.' Retain p3-example-2 to demonstrate an integer negative root.
Done when: The introductory examples contrast an integer root with a non-integer root expressed both exactly and approximately.

entries.description:
Simple Cubic Equations
• Cubic equations have unknowns to the power of 3: x³ “x cubed”
• Cube rooting ∛ is the inverse operation of cubing.
• A cubic equation in the form ax³ = k always has one real solution.
• Both positive and negative numbers can be cube rooted.
• To solve cubic equations:
1. Isolate x³.
2. Cube root both sides.
